The Death of Soil

By: John Webb | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
It's reported that soil in the U.S and Europe has between 30 and 40 years of fertility left, so how do we ensure we're able to feed ourselves if our farmers no longer can?

Unique Selling Point:
We need to find a different way of producing food if we're to stem some of the damage being done to the planet. The impact of pesticides on insect life and water sources is well-documented, as is the effect on soil fertility of "over-farming". These challenges aren't new, but the current Covid 19 epidemic has, in the minds of those with an eye on the bigger picture, re-emphasised a need to re-evaluate our relationship with the plant and what we demand of it. As difficult as it might be to focus on other crises given the turmoil created by the current one, we have a unique opportunity to reflect on the urgent action required to avoid the worst effects of human behaviour and how many people have already taken on the challenge.

Summary:
It's hard to keep up with the mounting crises threatening our planet- both present and future. Epidemics, climate change, over-population; has there been another generation that's faced as many existential challenges? Well, it would appear we need to add another to that growing list: the death of soil. It's not a new phenomenon. People have been warning for years that the intense and unrelenting use of cropland associated with industrial-scale farmland is robbing the soil of the nutrients it needs to sustain life. Nor is there consensus on when exactly the earth will say "this far and no further". But the Covid 19 crisis has brought into sharp relief the need to re-evaluate our relationship with the planet and how our actions - shaped as they might be by the noble intention to provide food, for example - are having devastating impacts.

Further information:
Enter Paul Hendrick, Ireland's Bee Guy: Organic/Vegan farmer, conservationist and activist. He's resuscitated a farm that was slowly dying - obliterated, like so many others, by modern farming practices relying on chemicals to ensure enough longevity to return a profit - and created a haven for bees and other insects. He's not going to save Ireland let alone the world, but he provides an example of the type of approach that'll be required to stave of the collapse of commercial agriculture. And the good news is that there are many others like him, now providing a practical and sustainable alternative rather than being ideological outliers.

Thousands of kms away from his farm in County Wicklow, a company is using a special kind of alchemy to entirely disconnect food production from agriculture. Solar Foods in Finland has produced a nutrient-rich protein (with the consistency of maize meal) using air and electricity. It is, in their words, the world's most environmentally-friendly food. It could also provide cheap sustenance more predictably that a warming planet is currently able to guarantee. Again, not the definitive solution but another example of people finding solutions before the gravest impacts of human behaviour take root.

These two stories will be augmented by a conversation with a South African/international expert who could provide the scientific background to soil's current predicament as well as an opinion on whether current predictions on its demise are accurate.

The intention is not to add to the alarmist clamour currently sweeping the globe but rather to acknowledge the challenge and suggest a new and more compassionate way of doing things.

Press Release:


Reaching Beyond Stars

When the most powerful radio telescope in the world – known as MeerKAT – was first set up, Carte Blanche was there. Now, we reveal some of the breathtaking discoveries astronomers have made using it. But these are only a foretaste of what the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) is all about. With construction set to begin this year, it’s one of the biggest collective scientific endeavours in history – to build the biggest radio telescope ever. This powerful telescope made up of thousands of collecting dishes spread out over 3000 km, will allow scientists to understand how the earliest stars and galaxies formed, reveal the nature of mysterious dark matter and perhaps even detect life elsewhere in the universe. Most of the SKA will be built in the Karoo and will make the small town of Carnarvon one of the premiere destinations for all of astronomy.

Producer: Julian Sun | Presenter: Derek Watts

Script: Death of Soil
Open with Meadow sequence and upsound – let it breath, gentle music, portrait shots into camera
Meadow Upsound – “Credit: Canola Pictures” “I live in County Wicklow in Ireland…”
VO: 6-year-old Meadow doesn’t realise it yet, but she changed her parent’s lives, and not just in the way children normally do.
Fade to black then back to portrait shot with upsound running underneath
Meadow Upsound – “We need the big people to start looking after animals and caring for them…”
Cut to drone family portrait then freeze and fade to sepia but leave Meadow in colour (1) then cut to short drone pan of landscape and into shots walking through the fields.
VO: Just a few short years ago, her mom and dad had planned to move the familly abroad, but then a chance encounter brought them here: a 55-acre farm in southern Ireland – up for sale and in need of TLC.
ITV Paul Handrick [01:01:23:08 - 01:01:36:08] We just fell in love with it, we couldn’t pass on it. So, we came in and the journey began.
VO: It was a journey into the unknown: transforming this place into a vegan-organic farm that made a little money, provided a sanctuary for nature and – most importantly – showed a commitment to a better world for Meadow and her siblings.
ITV Paul Handrick STRAP “Organic-Vegan Farmer” [01:03:49:15 - 01:04:11:06] we’re learning on the ground, we learn, we make mistakes, and we try and correct them [01:04:13:04 - 01:04:18:10 ] We come to it out of a place of integrity (CUT) That’s the main thing, we want to do the right thing.
VO: Like much of agricultural Ireland, this land was in decline: its soils robbed of nutrients from years over over-farming, any signs of insect life virtually wiped out by pesticides. Paul set about changing that. He’s doesn’t spray chemicals and he’s set aside meadows allowing nature to choose its own path. For him, it’s as much about being able to look his children in the eye, as it is helping to fix what he believes is a broken system.
Start building dramatic music under the end of his answer
ITV Paul Handrick [01:19:00:17 - 01:19:15:22] We need to get serious about it now (CUT) I'll probably get out of it in my lifetime without seeing too much trouble, but my youngest is six years of age, what would I say to her? Sorry we knew but we did nothing. That's not gonna cut it.
Dramatic factory farming footage – more intense music and tighter cuts (2)
VO: The world’s population is projected to reach 9 billion in the next 30 years. That’s a lot of mouths to feed and so, unsurprisingly, farming is increasingly looking like this. (PAUSE) Estimates put the number of farm animals reared for food globally at around 70 billion a year, and about two thirds of those are farmed intensively. Not all animal agriculture looks like this, but according to some reports there are 50 thousand of these places in the United States alone. They keep prices low, but the environmental and animal welfare impacts are significant (PAUSE)
GV’s of fertile croplands (beauty shots – more in Morality of Meat insert) – change in music
VO: But, if factory farms are the ugly stepsisters in this story, then surely this is Cinderella - hectare upon hectare of fertile cropland. Well, apparently not.
ITV Paul Handrick [01:31:21:00 - 01:31:53:07] If you know no better, it looks amazing you think this is great and everything's fine but when you look below the surface. It's not.
VO: Perhaps not so much below the surface, as on top of it.
LINK: What do you do to celebrate World Soil Day on the 5th of December every year? Ok, let me ask a different question: how many of you know that we celebrate World Soil Day on the 5th of December every year? Probably not many and, to be honest, up until yesterday I didn’t either.
ITV Bob Scholes [00:05:07:05 - 00:05:33:03] This is I have argued you know one of the more serious environmental problems facing the world today.
Scholes Establishers into erosion aerials
VO: Bob Scholes is a Professor of Systems Ecology at Wits and what he’s describing is as good a reason as any for having a soil day. In the past 200 hundred years, we’ve been depleting the soil faster than it’s been able to regenerate. It’s the result of a combination of things, many linked to questionable farming practices such as the use of heavy machinery and chemical spraying: around 2.5 billion kilogrammes of pesticide are used globally each year – mostly by farmers. But arguably the biggest driver of depletion or degradation is erosion – the actual removal of the topsoil caused by clearing for crops or grazing cattle.
ITV Bob Scholes “STRAP Professor: Systems Ecocology, WITS” We did a calculation two years ago about land degradation which of which soil erosion is a big component which showed that it is the single environmental crisis if you like of the contemporary time which affects the largest number of people right now. That's about 3 billion people.
VO: It takes hundreds of years to form a few cms of topsoil, but it’s being degraded at an alarming rate. According to Professor Scholes, South Africa is losing about 150 million tonnes per year to erosion alone.
ITV Bob Scholes STRAP “Professor: Systems Ecology, WITS” [00:02:57:03 - 00:03:30:02] To put that into perspective the rate at which soil is regenerated in our environment is about 10 million tonnes per year. In other words, we're losing soil at somewhere around about 15 times the rate at which we are replacing it.
GV’s or more of your drone shots – maybe into a rugby pitch graphic? (3)
VO: The international picture isn’t much different: the UN says we’re losing 30 soccer fields of soil every minute, mostly due to intensive farming. At current rates, it estimates the world’s topsoil could be gone within 60 years – although estimates differ widely. Professor Scholes has calculated that South Africa has longer than that.
ITV Bob Scholes [00:07:02:00 - 00:07:34:08] But the point is that in the time period of the next half century we come to this crunch point where the amount of food that we can produce because of climate change because of the finite size of the agricultural resource will hit a ceiling. And so even if we don't lose all the soil of the world even losing a small amount in that timeframe gives us a serious problem.
Into more industrial farming shots then cut to Paul on tractor or grader and his wife in garden.
VO: In the next 30 years we’ll need to ramp up production to feed a growing population, but the way we’ve been producing most of our crops and meat is unsustainable. But help is at hand: around the world people are hard at work trying to produce food more sustainably, some in ways a lot less conventional that what Paul is doing.
LINK: If what you see around me embodies the idea of working with rather than against nature, then a three hour flight from here – roughly in that direction – takes you to a place working to liberate food production by doing away with the need for agriculture entirely. (4)
Animate map and zoom into Hesinki. (5)
VO: At a facility in Finland’s capital, Helsinki, a bit of chemical wizardry is at play.
Upsound Juha Pitkänen - promo vid [00:00 – 00:07] You know, this might not look like much but it’s the start of a new era of food production.
Establishers of Juha from the promotional video
VO: Dr. Juha-Pekka Pitkänen is co-founder of a company making food out of thin air. It’s a process they hope will generate 400 million meals per year by 2025. It’s attracting a lot of attention – hence the slick promotional videos in which Dr. Pitkanen plays a starring role.
Upsound Juha Pitkänen - promo vid [00:25 – 00:30] This is a combination of science and nature and I’m here to explain what it means.
Footage from promo vid to demo process – [00:58 - 01:15] CREDIT: Solar Foods
VO: The process begins by cultivating billions of microbes in nature and encouraging them to grow and multiply – a bit like making yeast.
Footage from website https://solarfoods.fi/pressroom/material-bank/process/
VO: Once there’s enough of the microbe, they’re transferred to what’s known as a bio-reactor (video 1 and 2). But, like us, they need food and that’s where this device comes in: (video 7) it captures water and carbon di-oxide from air which is then given a blast of electricity to split the water into hydrogen and oxygen gasses – the resulting chemical concoction is the meal of choice for hungry microbes which, happily nourished, continue to grow.
Usound Juha Pitkänen - promo vid [02:36 – 02:39] Next, we move onto something pretty exciting… the harvest.
VO: After drying (video 8 and 9)…
Footage from the promo vid – [03:05 – 03:10] into Zoom shots and Pitkanen adjusting screen (6)
VO: …this is the result: a natural, sustainable protein called Solein (Soleen). Food from thin air - the link between agriculture and food production broken.
Usound Juha Pitkänen - promo vid [03:19 – 03:24] We’re following nature’s play book, we just like to do it a little more efficiently.
Into Zoom shots and Pitkanen adjusting screen (6)
VO: But a couple of nagging questions remained, so I linked up with Dr Pitkänen while at Paul’s farm.
John question USE Camera Shot [00:04:14:09 - 00:04:42:06] Does it taste good?
ITV Juha Pitkänen STRAP “Co-Founder, Solar Foods” it doesn't have a lot of taste (CUT) It has a bit of a “carroty” taste, in my opinion (CUT) It resembles a little bit like cornflour.
John Question [00:04:42:08 - 00:04:51:10] So this is not something that you would necessarily eat on its own it is something that you would use in a similar way to I guess to flower to to make other things that would add variety to your diet.
ITV Juha Pitkänen [00:04:52:02 - 00:05:09:12] Yes that's correct.
VO: If successful, it could help reduce our consumption of meat and dairy. And, if you’re wondering how that will aid the revival of soil, consider that livestock consume close to 34% of global crop production.
ITV Juha Pitkänen [00:26:49:13 - 00:26:54:02] I think meat eating will be kind of a speciality in the future (CUT) Maybe like a festive meal or something.
GVs and Prof Scholes cutaways.
VO: But, the not every solution to this crisis needs to rely on technology quite as extraordinary – or even startling - as this. In fact, they’re not unlike what we’re doing already – just, better.
ITV Bob Scholes [00:17:20:05 - 00:17:51:05] amongst all the things all the environmental crises which we have we are facing. This one is the easiest to solve. The solutions are well-known.”
VO: And, for Africa in particular, where agricultural land is still under-utilised, that even means ramping up production - but in a way that doesn’t repeat the mistakes of the past.
ITV Bob Scholes [00:15:19:20 - 00:16:05:16] we have an opportunity (CUT) leapfrog directly into a much more ecological form of agriculture (CUT) that involves mimicking the way natural ecosystems work because they've been able to conserve their soil for millennia.
VO: And though it’s still a work in progress…
ITV Paul Handrick [01:34:04:17 - 01:34:39:15] There's no secret recipe, it's actually slightly embarrassing how little you have to do - it's stepping back.
VO: A small farm in County Wicklow in Ireland, is helping to show the way.
ITV Paul Handrick [01:34:51:21 - 01:35:23:08] people say, “leave a strip for nature”. What we've done is take the strip for us and we leave the rest to nature.
Ends.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): It's reported that soil in the U.S and Europe has between 30 and 40 years of fertility left, so how do we ensure we're able to feed ourselves if our farmers no longer can?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We need to find a different way of producing food if we're to stem some of the damage being done to the planet. The impact of pesticides on insect life and water sources is well-documented, as is the effect on soil fertility of "over-farming". These challenges aren't new, but the current Covid 19 epidemic has, in the minds of those with an eye on the bigger picture, re-emphasised a need to re-evaluate our relationship with the plant and what we demand of it. As difficult as it might be to focus on other crises given the turmoil created by the current one, we have a unique opportunity to reflect on the urgent action required to avoid the worst effects of human behaviour and how many people have already taken on the challenge.
metadata.Summary: It's hard to keep up with the mounting crises threatening our planet- both present and future. Epidemics, climate change, over-population; has there been another generation that's faced as many existential challenges? Well, it would appear we need to add another to that growing list: the death of soil. It's not a new phenomenon. People have been warning for years that the intense and unrelenting use of cropland associated with industrial-scale farmland is robbing the soil of the nutrients it needs to sustain life. Nor is there consensus on when exactly the earth will say "this far and no further". But the Covid 19 crisis has brought into sharp relief the need to re-evaluate our relationship with the planet and how our actions - shaped as they might be by the noble intention to provide food, for example - are having devastating impacts.
metadata.Further information: Enter Paul Hendrick, Ireland's Bee Guy: Organic/Vegan farmer, conservationist and activist. He's resuscitated a farm that was slowly dying - obliterated, like so many others, by modern farming practices relying on chemicals to ensure enough longevity to return a profit - and created a haven for bees and other insects. He's not going to save Ireland let alone the world, but he provides an example of the type of approach that'll be required to stave of the collapse of commercial agriculture. And the good news is that there are many others like him, now providing a practical and sustainable alternative rather than being ideological outliers. Thousands of kms away from his farm in County Wicklow, a company is using a special kind of alchemy to entirely disconnect food production from agriculture. Solar Foods in Finland has produced a nutrient-rich protein (with the consistency of maize meal) using air and electricity. It is, in their words, the world's most environmentally-friendly food. It could also provide cheap sustenance more predictably that a warming planet is currently able to guarantee. Again, not the definitive solution but another example of people finding solutions before the gravest impacts of human behaviour take root. These two stories will be augmented by a conversation with a South African/international expert who could provide the scientific background to soil's current predicament as well as an opinion on whether current predictions on its demise are accurate. The intention is not to add to the alarmist clamour currently sweeping the globe but rather to acknowledge the challenge and suggest a new and more compassionate way of doing things.
